title: Two Pointers Pattern Explained: A LeetCode Guide (2026)
description: The two pointers pattern explained: the three shapes it takes, how to pick which pointer moves, when not to sort, and the six problems worth practising.
content:
The sorted array you are not using

Find two numbers in a sorted array that add up to a target. The obvious solution is two nested loops: for every number, scan the rest looking for its complement. It works, it is O(n²), and it throws away the single most useful fact in the problem statement — that the array is already sorted.

The two pointers pattern is what you do with that fact. It is the cheapest pattern to learn, it appears in more interviews than any other, and it usually turns O(n²) into O(n) with no extra memory at all.

The analogy: closing in from both ends

Imagine a shelf of books arranged by height, shortest on the left, tallest on the right. You want two books whose combined height is exactly one metre.

Put one hand on each end. Measure the pair. Too tall? The tallest book cannot possibly be in the answer with anything shorter still available on the left, so move the right hand inward. Too short? Nothing to the left of your left hand can help either, so move the left hand inward.

Every move eliminates an entire set of possibilities in one step. That is why a single pass is enough: each comparison rules out a whole row of the nested loop's search space rather than one cell of it.

The three shapes of two pointers

Most people learn the converging version and stop. There are three, and knowing which one a problem needs is most of the work.

Converging — pointers start at opposite ends and move toward each other

The classic. Requires sorted input, or a problem where "both ends" is meaningful. Pair with Target Sum, Valid Palindrome, Container With Most Water, 3Sum.

The loop condition is while left < right, and each iteration moves exactly one pointer inward based on a comparison. Because the pointers only ever move toward each other, the loop runs at most n times.

Fast and slow — both start at the left, one moves faster

Used for in-place work on arrays and for cycles in linked lists. In the array case, the slow pointer marks "where the next kept element goes" and the fast pointer scans ahead — that is Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array and Move Zeroes.

In the linked list case, one pointer takes one step and the other takes two. If there is a cycle, they must eventually meet, because the gap between them changes by exactly one each step. That is Linked List Cycle, and the same trick finds the middle of a list in a single pass.

Parallel — two pointers walking two different sequences

Merging two sorted arrays, checking whether one string is a subsequence of another, or comparing two versions. Each pointer advances through its own sequence according to a comparison.

The mess: sorting when you should not have

Two pointers usually requires sorted input, so the reflex becomes "sort it first". That reflex is wrong often enough to cost offers.

Sorting costs O(n log n). If the problem is Two Sum on an unsorted array and you only need the indices, a hash map solves it in O(n) — sorting first is strictly worse, and it destroys the original indices, which the problem asked for. Reaching for a sort here signals pattern-matching rather than thinking.

Sorting is right when the problem needs relative order rather than positions: 3Sum, or any problem where you must skip duplicates, or Container With Most Water where the geometry depends on both ends. The tell is whether the answer is a set of values or a set of indices.

The fix: let the invariant choose the pointer

The mechanical part of two pointers is deciding which pointer to move. There is a reliable way to get it right every time: state the invariant, then ask which move preserves it.

For Pair with Target Sum on a sorted array, the invariant is "the answer, if it exists, lies between left and right inclusive". If arr[left] + arr[right] is too large, then arr[right] is too large to pair with anything remaining, because everything left of right is smaller. So right cannot be part of the answer and can be discarded. Move it inward. The symmetric argument moves left.

For Container With Most Water the invariant is different — the area is bounded by the shorter wall, so moving the taller one inward can never help, since the width shrinks and the height is still capped by the short wall. Always move the shorter one.

Being able to say "here is my invariant, and here is why this move preserves it" is the difference between a candidate who has memorised the loop and one who can adapt it when the interviewer changes the problem.

3Sum, and the duplicate problem

3Sum is where two pointers stops being a warm-up. The structure is a loop plus a two-pointer scan: fix the first number, then find a pair in the remainder summing to its negation. That is O(n²), which is optimal for this problem, and it is the standard example of nesting a pointer scan inside an outer loop.

The part candidates get wrong is duplicates. The problem asks for unique triplets, and a sorted array makes duplicates adjacent, so you skip them in two places: after fixing the outer element, and after recording a match, advancing both inner pointers past any repeated values.

Say this out loud while coding it. "I am sorting so that duplicates sit next to each other, which lets me skip them in O(1) instead of deduplicating a result set afterwards." That single sentence justifies the sort, explains the skip logic, and pre-empts the follow-up question.

The six problems worth doing

  1. Pair with Target Sum — the converging template, unadorned.
  2. Valid Palindrome — converging with a character filter; teaches clean edge handling.
  3. Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array — the fast/slow in-place write pattern.
  4. Container With Most Water — a different invariant, and the best test of whether you understand why a move is safe.
  5. 3Sum — nesting, plus duplicate skipping.
  6. Sort Colors — the Dutch national flag problem, with three pointers and one pass.

Sort Colors is worth the extra effort. It is the natural bridge to problems where the array is partitioned in place, and it is a common follow-up when an interviewer wants to see whether your two-pointer instinct generalises.

How to talk about this in an interview

A thirty-second answer:

"The brute force is two nested loops, O(n²). But the array is sorted, and I am not using that. If I put one pointer at each end, the sum tells me which pointer to move: too large means the right element is too big to pair with anything remaining, so I move it inward; too small means the left element is too small. Each pointer only moves inward, so the whole thing is one pass — O(n) time and O(1) extra space."

Notice the shape: brute force, the unused fact, the invariant, the move rule, the complexity. That sequence works for every two-pointer problem you will be given.

Key Takeaways

  • Two pointers replaces a nested loop by using an ordering fact the brute force ignores — usually that the input is sorted.
  • There are three shapes: converging from both ends, fast and slow from the same end, and parallel across two sequences.
  • Do not sort reflexively. If the answer is indices rather than values, a hash map is usually the better O(n) tool.
  • Decide which pointer to move by stating the invariant and asking which move preserves it — that reasoning is what gets scored.
  • In 3Sum, sorting is what makes duplicate skipping cheap. Say so while you code it.
